passage: At the end of the day at playschool, the van was honking outside. Kalyani sat on the low bench with one sandal on the wrong foot. Ritu Miss knelt to help. "No! Me do it!" Kalyani pulled her foot away. She tugged the strap, it slipped, she tugged again. Her tongue poked out. Ritu Miss sat back on her heels, waited, and called to the driver, "Two more minutes!" At last the strap clicked. Kalyani stood up, stamped both feet, and marched to the van, chin high.

qa.q: What did Kalyani say when Ritu Miss knelt to help?
qa.a: "No! Me do it!"

qa.q: What does Kalyani's stamping and chin held high suggest she felt?
qa.a: She felt proud and strong because she had done the strap by herself 😊.

qa.q: What choice did Ritu Miss make, and why was it a good one?
qa.a: She sat back, waited and asked the driver for two more minutes, letting Kalyani finish on her own.

qa.q: How might the van driver feel about the two extra minutes?
qa.a: The driver may be a bit impatient, but a short wait lets a small child leave feeling capable instead of upset.

grounding: A small girl at playschool insists on doing her own sandal strap while the van waits.

passage: I'm Mahima, Deepak's big sister. Every morning before school Papa says, "Quick, quick, we're late!" and every morning Deepak sits on the doorstep with his shoes and says, "I do it." He puts the left shoe on the right foot. He tries again. The laces are like noodles in his hands. Papa taps his watch. Today Papa reached down, and Deepak cried, "Mine!" and hugged his shoe. So Papa waited. When the last lace was a floppy bow, Deepak held up his foot like a trophy. We were late. He didn't care one bit.

qa.q: What did Deepak do when Papa reached down to help?
qa.a: Deepak cried, "Mine!" and hugged his shoe.

qa.q: Why did Deepak hold up his foot like a trophy?
qa.a: He felt proud that he'd done it himself, and that mattered more to him than being on time.

qa.q: What could Papa try on school mornings so Deepak can still do it himself?
qa.a: Papa could start shoe time a few minutes earlier, so Deepak can keep his 'I do it' without everyone rushing.

qa.q: How does Mahima see these mornings?
qa.a: Mahima watches with some amusement, noticing Papa's watch-tapping and Deepak not caring one bit about being late.

grounding: A big sister describes her small brother insisting on putting on his own shoes even when the family is late.

passage:
Monday: Vasudha's mother, Parul, was late for the bus and pushed Vasudha's feet into her shoes. Vasudha kicked and cried all the way to the stop. "I wanted to do it!"
Wednesday: Parul put the shoes out early by the door and said nothing. Vasudha sat and worked on them for a long time, grunting, the velcro sticking crooked. They were five minutes late. Vasudha was smiling.
Friday: Vasudha put her shoes on by herself, still crooked, and ran to show her mother. "Look! I did it all!" Parul laughed and fixed nothing.

qa.q: Where did Parul put the shoes on Wednesday?
qa.a: She put the shoes out early by the door.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha kick and cry on Monday?
qa.a: Vasudha felt angry and frustrated because she wanted to do it herself, and having her feet pushed into the shoes took that away.

qa.q: What change did Parul make, and why did it work?
qa.a: She set the shoes out early and stayed quiet, giving Vasudha time and space to do it by herself.

qa.q: How might Parul's week feel compared with Vasudha's?
qa.a: Parul feels the pressure of being late, but on Friday she sees her daughter proud and happy, which makes the waiting worth it.

grounding: Across a week, a small girl insists on doing her own shoes, and her mother makes room for it.

passage:
Rain drummed on the tin shade, and the school van was already honking at the gate. Yusuf held out Reena's shoes. 'Quick, Abbu will do it.'
'NO. Me do it.' Reena sat on the step and pushed the left shoe onto the right foot. Took it off. Tried again. Her tongue poked out.
Yusuf looked at the clock and breathed out. He crouched and held the shoe still, just still, while Reena pushed her foot in.
She stood up, stamped both feet and beamed. 'I did it!'
They ran through the puddles to the van, two minutes late.

qa.q: What was the weather while Reena put on her shoes?
qa.a: Rain was drumming on the tin shade.

qa.q: Why did Reena shout 'Me do it'?
qa.a: She badly wanted to do it herself; managing her own shoes made her feel big and capable, even with the van honking.

qa.q: What choice did Yusuf make that helped, and why did it work?
qa.a: Instead of taking over, he held the shoe still while Reena pushed her foot in; she still did it herself, and they were only two minutes late.

qa.q: What would change for Reena if Yusuf had just put the shoes on for her?
qa.a: They might have caught the van on time, but Reena would likely have protested and missed that proud 'I did it!' moment.

grounding: A young child insists on putting on her own shoes while the van honks, and her father steadies the shoe instead of taking over.

passage:
In the lift lobby of their Pune building, the whole family was ready for Nani's birthday lunch, except for Parveen's shoes. The cab driver had called twice.
'Let me,' said Ujjwal bhaiya, bending down.
'I can DO it!' Parveen pulled the foot away and started on the buckle, missing the hole again and again.
Mumma opened her mouth, then shut it. 'Okay. Buckle's yours. Bhaiya holds the lift.'
Ujjwal held the lift door. Pin, hole, miss. Pin, hole... click.
Parveen looked up, face shining. 'Done! By myself!'
In the cab, Parveen kept swinging both feet to admire the buckles.

qa.q: Who held the lift door?
qa.a: Ujjwal bhaiya.

qa.q: Why did Parveen pull the foot away from Ujjwal bhaiya?
qa.a: Parveen wanted to do the buckle alone; doing it 'by myself' mattered more than being quick.

qa.q: What choice did Mumma make, and why was it a good one?
qa.a: Mumma gave Parveen the buckle and gave Ujjwal bhaiya the lift, so Parveen could finish while the family kept moving.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal bhaiya feel being pushed away when trying to help?
qa.a: He may feel a little brushed off, with the cab waiting, but holding the lift gave him a useful job as well.

grounding: A young child insists on doing a shoe buckle alone while the family is late, and a parent makes room for it.
